title: Pool vs session-slot econ (scratchpad)
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad contrasting two operational/pricing metaphors for serving interactive inference: 1) prewarmed pool (reserved slots / prewarmed contexts) and 2) session-slot (on-demand per-session allocation).

High-level goal:
- Find clean heuristics to translate infra-level costs (GPU hours, prewarm slots, cold-start overhead) into customer-visible units that map to usage patterns: micro-interactions, long-lived chats, and bursty API usage.

Assumptions (back-of-envelope, changeable):
- Base infra amortized cost per prewarmed slot: $1.50 / hour (represents portion of GPU + infra + networking + ops).
- Effective sustained token throughput per active slot (for typical generation workload): 30 tokens/sec => ~108k tokens/hour.
- Cold-start extra GPU work: ~2s of additional active GPU time (model load/kv-setup/higher latency window) for a session that didn't find a warm slot.
- Average session length scenarios: micro (3 requests, 15s total), medium chat (30 requests, 5 min), long conversation (200 requests, 45 min).
- Typical cache hit (prefix/KV reuse) inside a session: 80% for multi-turn chat (reduces per-token compute by ~some factor).

Core math (derivations):
- Per-token cost from a prewarmed slot: 1.5 $/hr / 108k tokens = $0.0000139 per token => $0.0139 per 1k tokens.
- Cold-start incremental cost per session (if no warm slot): 2s * $1.50/hr / 3600s = $0.0008333 per session.
- If session is micro (15s total), cold-start cost is large relative to payload tokens: e.g., 15s * 30 tps = 450 tokens; cold-start adds $0.00083 => incremental $0.00185 per 1k tokens for that session (on top of baseline token cost).

Pool model (reserved prewarmed slots):
- Mechanics: customer commits to N prewarmed slots per region / model class. Those slots are always available for their traffic. Unused minutes are effectively paid for.
- Pros: near-zero cold-start latency; predictable throughput/latency; simple to reason about SLOs.
- Cons: worse fit for bursty, low-util customers unless slot-sharing across tenants allowed.
- Pricing levers to offer: 1) flat monthly charge per-slot (e.g., $1.50/hr * 24 * 30 = $1080/mo per slot) with volume discounts for multi-slot commitments; 2) hybrid: slot rental + per-token lower rate.
- Example: slot base + discounted token: slot base $1080/mo + token rate $0.009 / 1k tokens. This favors high-throughput customers and guarantees capacity.

Session-slot model (on-demand slots with cold penalty):
- Mechanics: sessions request a slot on demand. If an idle slot available, attach; otherwise cold-start (slower). We bill per-session overhead + tokens or per-request ephemeral slot minutes.
- Pros: economical for highly bursty/low-duty users; simple pay-as-you-go.
- Cons: unpredictable tail latencies, more complex QoS.
- Pricing levers: 1) per-session connection fee (to cover cold-start amortization) 2) higher per-token rate for completely on-demand (reflects tail latency costs) 3) session-duration discounts.
- Example pricing: per-session fee = $0.001 (covers ~1.2s of overhead). Token rate = $0.02 / 1k tokens for on-demand. For long sessions, per-token cost converges toward prewarmed slot economics when session length >> amortized cold-start.

Hybrid ideas (practical products):
- Burst buffer: customer pre-buys a small pool of prewarmed credits (e.g., 10 slot-minutes) that automatically cover initial N sessions each minute, reducing cold starts while avoiding full slot commitment.
- Auto-commit step: convert observed usage into recommended slot-commitment (ML heuristic) and offer a discount window to customer for committing.
- Session credit bundling: sell bundles of "prewarm credits" that cover cold-starts (each credit ~= 2s of prewarm cost). Useful for customers that want steady 99th %ile latency without reserving full slots.

Back-of-envelope scenarios (sanity checks):
1) Small app, 10k tokens/day (~$0.14/day if prepaid slot $0.0139/1k): PAYG token-only makes sense.
2) Mid-size app, 100M tokens/month: token-only at $0.0139/1k => $1,390/month. If they need <100ms cold-start SLOs, one slot reserved (108k tokens/hr) can cover sustained traffic but not spiky bursts. The slot monthly math: $1080/mo per slot; if they need 8 slots steady = $8,640/mo — compare to token-only $1,390 => token-only cheaper unless customer requires SLOs or high concurrency.
3) Very latency-sensitive, 500 RPS bursts (short windows): pool model preferred; per-slot amortization + concurrency planning needed.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Better estimate of "cold-start GPU time" across model sizes + quantization levels (2s is placeholder). Measure across typical models (7B, 13B, 70B).
- Validate 30 tps figure under our batching/runtime. Provide per-model throughput map.
- Simulate customer mixes (bursty vs steady) to find break-even points between token-only vs 1 slot vs N slots.
- UX: how to present "prewarm credits" to users in Console so it’s understandable.
- Edge case: multi-tenant slots vs dedicated slots — how to price sharing safely while preserving SLOs.

Notes to self / next steps:
- Run quick script to compute per-token economics for 7B/13B/70B using measured tps and model memory footprint.
- Draft short Console copy for 3 options: PAYG tokens, Hybrid prewarm credits, Reserved slot commitments.
- Sync with Diego on slot scheduling constraints and Harpreet on product/legal language for committing slots.

Slack refs / tickets to attach later:
- linear: ISSUE-342 (slot scheduling), JIRA-ish: RINF-768 (pricing experiments).

Random thoughts:
- Could offer "session-duration floors" (first 30s billed at min cost to cover cold-start overhead) which smooths per-request friction for tiny sessions.
- Consider regional price differences: prewarm slots in us-west cheaper than eu-west due to infra. Tie discounting to region-specific capacity.

Bottom line (working thesis):
- For most customers, a lightweight hybrid (small bundle of prewarm credits + clear per-token PAYG) will cover 80% of use cases. Full slot commitments should be targeted for customers with consistent throughput or strict SLOs.
